title: Just Meet Them Once
excerpt: On wedding gifts with price tags, the family name, and what happens at breakfast after someone says no.
content:
“Just meet them once.” It sounds like such a small favour. One cup of tea, one Sunday afternoon. What bothers me is what can happen after the tea. Someone has already told an aunt. The aunt has told the other family how excited everyone is. By Monday, the one person who still has a decision to make is being asked how they could possibly disappoint so many people.

I can understand a parent wanting company for their child. I can even understand the quiet fear underneath “Who will look after you when we’re gone?” There’s affection in introducing two people who might like each other. The test comes the morning after, when one of them says, “They were lovely. I don’t want a second meeting.” How does the family treat them at breakfast?

In some Indian families, a wedding carries so many other ambitions that an ordinary no can sound like a financial disaster. A son has a good job abroad. Somebody mentions how much his parents spent on his education. Then somebody mentions a car. Nobody wants to say out loud what a car has to do with two people liking each other. Yet the bride’s parents know exactly who is expected to pay, and roughly what it would cost their daughter if they declined. Calling it a gift is easy for the person choosing the model.

There’s a quieter kind of profit, too. Imagine a daughter-in-law who works a full day and then comes home to cook for six. She may love those six people. She may also want a Tuesday evening to herself. If taking that evening makes her selfish, the family has quietly written her labour into the marriage agreement. She was the last person to see the terms.

And then comes the family name. I always wonder what people actually want to carry forward when they say that. A grandmother’s way of folding a paratha? The habit of putting an extra plate on the table because someone might turn up? Those are things I’d want to inherit. A surname can survive perfectly well on paper while everybody who bears it dreads coming home. Asking a couple to have a child so a name can last another generation is asking an awful lot of three people, one of whom hasn’t even arrived.

What I’d love to hear more often is a parent telling the relatives, “I made the introduction. They’ve given me their answer.” Then changing the subject. No family summit, no revised sales pitch, no aunt calling privately to ask what went wrong.

And on Sunday, set out the tea again. Let the kid come over late, eat the good biscuits, complain about work and go home carrying leftovers. That ordinary welcome, after they’ve chosen something you wouldn’t have chosen for them, seems to me a family tradition worth keeping.
